claims.text: In-situ HTXRD can reveal oxidation-induced phase evolution in the additive-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA.
In-situ HTXRD can reveal elemental redistribution within nanoprecipitates in this HEA.
The additive-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA contains a fine-scale dual-nanoprecipitate distribution in a predominantly solid-solution matrix.
The nanoprecipitates may serve as nucleation sites for oxide formation.
The nanoprecipitates may influence the distribution of oxidizing species.
High-temperature oxidation selectively alters nanoprecipitate phases in this alloy.
High-temperature oxidation drives elemental migration between the nanoprecipitates and matrix.
In-situ HTXRD can identify time- and temperature-dependent phase formation or transformation during high-temperature oxidation.
Changes in diffraction peak positions, intensities, and the emergence of new peaks can indicate phase evolution during oxidation.
Diffraction-peak evolution can establish elemental redistribution between nanoprecipitates and the matrix.
Oxidation will produce time-dependent changes in the in-situ diffraction patterns.
Protective Cr- or Al-based oxides may appear during oxidation of the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA.
Nanoprecipitate-phase changes will correlate with improved or degraded oxidation resistance relative to cast or wrought material.
Cast or wrought versions of the same HEA lack the fine dual-nanoprecipitate microstructure.
Oxidation-induced phase transformations are less pronounced in cast or wrought versions of the alloy.
In-situ HTXRD may not resolve sub-nanometer-scale elemental changes.
Overlapping diffraction signals in a multiphase alloy may prevent unambiguous phase identification without complementary techniques.
Elemental redistribution cannot necessarily be quantified precisely from diffraction data alone.
Ex-situ TEM-EDS can independently test the proposed elemental redistribution.
